q: Name the pinned muscle running straight down the middle of the front of the thigh.
options: Vastus intermedius
Sartorius
Rectus femoris
Vastus lateralis

why.correct: The rectus femoris runs straight down the middle of the front of the thigh from the ilium to the quadriceps tendon. It is the only part of the quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip.
options: The vastus intermedius lies deep, hidden under the rectus femoris.
The sartorius crosses the thigh diagonally, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia.
Correct. The straight middle muscle is the rectus femoris.
The vastus lateralis is on the outer side of the thigh.

q: Name the pinned long, thin strap crossing the front of the thigh diagonally.
options: Sartorius
Gracilis
Adductor longus
Tensor fasciae latae

why.correct: The sartorius runs diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial surface of the upper tibia. It is the longest muscle in the body.
options: Correct. The diagonal strap is the sartorius.
The gracilis is a thin strap too, but it runs straight down the inner thigh from the pubis.
The adductor longus is a short triangular muscle high on the inner thigh.
The tensor fasciae latae is a short muscle on the outer front of the hip.

q: Name the pinned slender muscle along the inner edge of the thigh.
options: Sartorius
Semitendinosus
Adductor magnus
Gracilis

why.correct: The gracilis (slender) runs from the lower pubis straight down the inner thigh to the medial surface of the upper tibia. It adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
options: The sartorius runs diagonally across the front of the thigh, not straight down the inner edge.
The semitendinosus is on the back of the thigh, starting on the ischial tuberosity.
The adductor magnus is a large, deep muscle inserting along the femur, not a thin strap reaching the tibia.
Correct. The slender inner-thigh strap is the gracilis.

q: On the back of the thigh, name the pinned lateral hamstring.
options: Semimembranosus
Biceps femoris
Semitendinosus
Vastus lateralis

why.correct: The biceps femoris is the lateral hamstring. Its long head starts on the ischial tuberosity and its short head on the linea aspera; it inserts on the head of the fibula.
options: The semimembranosus is a medial hamstring.
Correct. The lateral hamstring is the biceps femoris.
The semitendinosus is a medial hamstring, with a long cord-like tendon.
The vastus lateralis is on the outer front of the thigh, part of the quadriceps femoris.

q: With the buttock muscles cut away, name the pinned pear-shaped muscle running from the sacrum to the greater trochanter.
options: Gluteus minimus
Quadratus lumborum
Piriformis
Iliacus

why.correct: The piriformis runs from the front of the sacrum to the greater trochanter and rotates the thigh laterally. A large nerve leaves the pelvis just below it.
options: The gluteus minimus lies higher on the outer ilium, fanning down to the front of the greater trochanter.
The quadratus lumborum is in the back wall of the abdomen, between the iliac crest and the twelfth rib.
Correct. This is the piriformis.
The iliacus lines the inner bowl of the ilium, on the front of the pelvis.

q: Name the pinned muscle on the front of the leg, just lateral to the shin.
options: Tibialis anterior
Fibularis longus
Extensor digitorum longus
Soleus

why.correct: The tibialis anterior lies along the lateral surface of the tibia and inserts on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal. It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
options: Correct. The muscle beside the shin is the tibialis anterior.
The fibularis longus is on the lateral side of the leg, over the fibula.
The extensor digitorum longus lies lateral to the tibialis anterior and runs to the toes.
The soleus is on the back of the leg, under the gastrocnemius.

q: On the back of the leg, name the pinned broad flat muscle beneath the two heads of the calf muscle.
options: Gastrocnemius
Tibialis posterior
Soleus
Biceps femoris

why.correct: The soleus lies under the gastrocnemius, from the head of the fibula and back of the tibia to the calcaneal tendon. It crosses only the ankle and plantar flexes the foot.
options: The gastrocnemius is the two-headed superficial calf muscle that lies over it.
The tibialis posterior is the deepest muscle of the back of the leg.
Correct. The broad muscle under the gastrocnemius is the soleus.
The biceps femoris is a hamstring on the back of the thigh.

q: Name the pinned muscle on the lateral side of the leg, over the fibula.
options: Tibialis anterior
Fibularis longus
Extensor digitorum longus
Gastrocnemius

why.correct: The fibularis longus runs from the head and upper fibula; its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the sole. It everts the foot.
options: The tibialis anterior lies on the front of the leg, beside the tibia.
Correct. The muscle over the fibula is the fibularis longus.
The extensor digitorum longus lies on the front of the leg and runs to the toes.
The gastrocnemius is the calf muscle on the back of the leg.

q: Name the pinned muscle that runs from the lumbar vertebrae down in front of the hip.
options: Iliacus
Quadratus lumborum
Psoas major
Pectineus

why.correct: The psoas major starts on the lumbar vertebrae and joins the iliacus to insert on the lesser trochanter. Together they form the iliopsoas, the prime mover of hip flexion.
options: The iliacus starts in the iliac fossa, the bowl of the ilium, not on the vertebrae.
The quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest up to the twelfth rib and does not cross the hip.
Correct. The muscle from the lumbar spine is the psoas major.
The pectineus is a short muscle from the pubis to just below the lesser trochanter.

q: Six hours after a tibia fracture was set, a 22-year-old soccer player has severe pain in the front of his leg, far worse than expected, and it gets much worse when the nurse gently points his toes downward. His foot pulse can still be felt. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Compartment syndrome of the anterior compartment of the leg
Rupture of the calcaneal tendon
A hamstring strain
Normal healing pain, since his pulse is present

why.correct: Bleeding and swelling inside the anterior compartment, wrapped in deep fascia that cannot stretch, raise the pressure until blood cannot flow through the capillaries. Pain out of proportion to the injury, and pain when the compartment's muscles are passively stretched (pointing the toes stretches the dorsiflexors), are the early signs. A pulse is often still present.
options: Correct. This is compartment syndrome of the front of the leg.
A calcaneal tendon rupture causes weakness rising onto the toes and pain at the back of the ankle, not severe pain in the front of the leg.
The hamstrings are on the back of the thigh, not the front of the leg.
A present pulse does not rule it out: the pressure in the large artery is far higher than the pressure in the compartment, so the pulse is often felt until late.

q: Which muscles belong to the quadriceps femoris? Select all that apply.
options: Rectus femoris
Vastus lateralis
Sartorius
Vastus medialis
Vastus intermedius
Biceps femoris

why.correct: The quadriceps femoris is four muscles: the rectus femoris and the vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius. All four insert through the quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar ligament on the tibial tuberosity.
options: Yes. The rectus femoris is the one part that crosses the hip.
Yes. The vastus lateralis is on the outer thigh.
No. The sartorius is also in the front of the thigh, but it inserts on the medial tibia and is not part of the quadriceps.
Yes. The vastus medialis is on the inner thigh above the knee.
Yes. The vastus intermedius lies deep under the rectus femoris.
No. The biceps femoris is a hamstring, on the back of the thigh.

q: When a patient stands on her right leg, the left side of her pelvis drops. Weakness of which muscle best explains this?
options: Left gluteus maximus
Right gluteus medius
Right iliopsoas
Left adductor longus

why.correct: Standing on the right leg, the body's weight hangs to the left of the right hip. The right gluteus medius and minimus, abductors of the standing leg, pull the ilium down toward the greater trochanter and hold the pelvis level. When they are weak, the opposite side drops: a positive Trendelenburg sign.
options: The gluteus maximus mainly extends the hip, and the muscle that levels the pelvis belongs to the standing leg, here the right.
Correct. The standing leg's gluteus medius holds the pelvis level.
The iliopsoas flexes the hip; it does not hold the pelvis level in standing.
The adductor longus adducts the thigh and belongs to the lifted leg; it cannot hold up the pelvis on this side.

q: A nurse gives a routine vaccine to a 4-month-old infant. Which site is preferred?
options: Deltoid site
Dorsogluteal site
Vastus lateralis site
The gastrocnemius

why.correct: An infant's thigh muscles are well developed while the gluteal and deltoid muscles are still small, so the middle third of the vastus lateralis on the outer thigh is the preferred site.
options: The deltoid is the usual vaccine site in adults, but in young infants it is too small.
The dorsogluteal site is avoided at every age: a large nerve lies close by and the fat layer is thick.
Correct. The vastus lateralis is preferred in infants.
The calf is not a standard injection site.

q: To find the ventrogluteal site, where does the heel of the nurse's hand go?
options: On the greater trochanter
On the anterior superior iliac spine
On the ischial tuberosity
On the iliac crest at the back

why.correct: The heel of the hand rests on the greater trochanter, the index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine and the middle finger spreads back along the iliac crest. The needle goes into the center of the V between the fingers, into the gluteus medius and minimus.
options: Correct. The heel of the hand goes on the greater trochanter.
The index finger, not the heel of the hand, goes on the anterior superior iliac spine.
The ischial tuberosity is the bone you sit on, far below the site.
The middle finger points back along the iliac crest; the heel of the hand is lower, on the femur.

q: A tennis player ruptures his right calcaneal tendon. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Ability to rise onto the toes of the right foot
variables.why: Rising onto the toes needs the gastrocnemius and soleus to pull the calcaneus up, and their shared tendon no longer connects them to it.

variables.name: Strength of pointing the right foot downward (plantar flexion)
variables.why: The main plantar flexors act through the calcaneal tendon. Only smaller muscles such as the tibialis posterior and the fibularis muscles are left to help.

variables.name: Strength of lifting the right toes toward the shin (dorsiflexion)
variables.why: Dorsiflexion is done by the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus on the front of the leg, which are unaffected.

why.correct: The gastrocnemius and soleus pull on the calcaneus only through the calcaneal tendon. With it ruptured, plantar flexion is weak and rising onto the toes fails, while the dorsiflexors on the front of the leg work normally.

q: Order the structures the pull of the quadriceps femoris passes through, from the muscle to its bony insertion.
options: Rectus femoris and the three vasti
Quadriceps tendon
Patella
Patellar ligament
Tibial tuberosity

why.correct: The four muscles join the quadriceps tendon, which wraps the patella; below the patella it continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
options: The four parts of the quadriceps femoris generate the pull.
They converge on the shared quadriceps tendon above the knee.
The patella is a sesamoid bone within the tendon.
Below the patella, the band is called the patellar ligament.
It inserts on the tibial tuberosity, below the knee.

q: Borders of the femoral triangle: the inguinal ligament above; the sartorius on the lateral side; the ____ on the medial side.
options: Gracilis
Adductor longus
Rectus femoris
Iliopsoas

why.correct: The medial border of the femoral triangle is the adductor longus, the most anterior of the adductors.
options: The gracilis lies farther medially along the inner thigh; it does not form a border of the triangle.
Correct. The adductor longus forms the medial border.
The rectus femoris runs down the middle of the thigh, lateral to the triangle.
The iliopsoas lies in the floor of the triangle, not along its medial border.

q: This traces the hamstrings from origin to insertion. One step is wrong. Find it.
options: All three originate on the ischial tuberosity
They run down the back of the thigh, behind the hip joint
They cross behind the knee joint
They insert on the tibial tuberosity

why.correct: The hamstrings insert behind the knee's axis, on the head of the fibula (biceps femoris) and the medial tibia (semitendinosus and semimembranosus). The tibial tuberosity, on the front of the tibia, is where the quadriceps femoris inserts.
options: Correct step. The ischial tuberosity is the hamstrings' shared origin.
Correct step. Running behind the hip, they extend it.
Correct step. Crossing behind the knee, they flex it.
This is the wrong step. They insert on the fibula and medial tibia, not the tibial tuberosity.

q: In which position are the hamstrings stretched the most, putting them at greatest risk of a strain?
options: Hip extended and knee flexed
Hip flexed and knee flexed
Hip extended and knee straight
Hip flexed and knee straight

why.correct: The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee, so they are lengthened by the opposite movements: hip flexion and knee extension. Doing both at once, as at the end of a sprinter's forward leg swing, stretches them at both ends.
options: Hip extension and knee flexion are the hamstrings' own actions, which shorten them.
Knee flexion shortens the hamstrings at their lower end, relieving some of the stretch from hip flexion.
Hip extension shortens them at the upper end, relieving the stretch from a straight knee.
Correct. Hip flexed with the knee straight stretches them the most.

q: Which muscle is the prime mover of hip flexion, lifting the knee toward the chest?
options: Gluteus maximus
Iliopsoas
Biceps femoris
Gluteus medius

why.correct: The iliopsoas (psoas major plus iliacus) passes in front of the hip joint to the lesser trochanter and is the prime mover of hip flexion.
options: The gluteus maximus is the prime mover of hip extension, the opposite movement.
Correct. The iliopsoas flexes the hip.
The biceps femoris extends the hip and flexes the knee.
The gluteus medius abducts the thigh and holds the pelvis level.

q: Walking on a sloping trail, you turn the soles of your feet outward to keep them flat. Which muscles are producing this eversion?
options: Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Fibularis longus and fibularis brevis
Extensor digitorum longus and sartorius

why.correct: The fibularis longus and brevis, in the lateral group of the leg, pass behind the lateral malleolus to the foot and turn the sole outward.
options: Both tibialis muscles invert the foot, turning the sole inward.
The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the foot through the calcaneal tendon.
Correct. The fibularis muscles evert the foot.
The extensor digitorum longus mainly extends the toes, and the sartorius acts at the hip and knee, not the foot.

q: Why is the dorsogluteal site, in the upper outer buttock, avoided for intramuscular injections?
options: The gluteus maximus there is too thin to hold an injection
The site has no bony landmarks at all
Muscle there absorbs drugs faster than any other site
A large nerve leaving the pelvis below the piriformis runs nearby, and the thick fat layer often keeps the needle from reaching muscle

why.correct: The body's largest nerve runs out of the pelvis below the piriformis, close to this site, and a thick layer of fat over the gluteus maximus means the needle may not reach muscle. The ventrogluteal site avoids both problems.
options: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body; thickness is not the problem.
It has landmarks (the posterior superior iliac spine and greater trochanter), but they are harder to use, and the nearby nerve is the main risk.
Faster absorption would not be a reason to avoid it; the risks are the nerve and the fat.
Correct. A nearby large nerve and thick fat make it risky.

q: Which fascial compartment contains the adductor longus, adductor magnus and gracilis?
options: Anterior compartment of the thigh
Medial compartment of the thigh
Posterior compartment of the thigh
Lateral compartment of the leg

why.correct: The adductors and gracilis sit together in the medial compartment of the thigh and share one main action: adducting the thigh.
options: The anterior compartment of the thigh holds the quadriceps femoris and sartorius, which extend the knee.
Correct. The adductors form the medial compartment.
The posterior compartment of the thigh holds the hamstrings.
The lateral compartment of the leg holds the fibularis muscles, below the knee.

q: Which structures form the lower borders of the popliteal fossa behind the knee?
options: The tendons of the hamstrings
The two heads of the gastrocnemius
The soleus and tibialis posterior
The patella and patellar ligament

why.correct: The popliteal fossa is a diamond. The hamstring tendons form its upper borders (biceps femoris laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially), and the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius form its lower borders.
options: The hamstring tendons form the upper borders, not the lower ones.
Correct. The two heads of the gastrocnemius form the lower borders.
The soleus and tibialis posterior lie deeper and lower in the calf, below the fossa.
The patella and patellar ligament are on the front of the knee.
